title: What is a bond?
subtitle: A basic debt instrument - you lend, they pay interest
openingQuestion: How does buying a bond differ from buying a stock?
openingOptions: Stocks are safer because they can be sold at any time
No difference - both are just securities on the exchange
Bonds simply cost more to buy than shares in the very same company
A bond lends money for fixed interest; a stock buys ownership
explanation: A bond is a loan that has been divided into tradable units: the issuer receives the money and commits to paying periodic interest and returning the face value at maturity. The buyer is a creditor, not an owner, so they get paid before shareholders if the business goes bankrupt, but they don't share in any growth upside. Three elements shape every bond - face value, coupon rate, and maturity - and every concept that follows revolves around these three.

diagram.label: The issuer needs capital, sells a bond
The investor pays for it, becomes a creditor
Receives periodic coupons throughout the term
Maturity: gets back the face value - and is paid before shareholders in bankruptcy

realWorldExample.description: When the Vietnam State Treasury issues a government bond, it is essentially the state borrowing money from investors (including banks, investment funds, and individuals) with a commitment to pay periodic interest and return the principal at maturity - one of the government's largest capital-raising tools.

quiz.question: Coupon rate is 5%, face value is 1 million. How much interest is received each year?
options: 25,000 VND (= 5% × 1,000,000 VND ÷ 2, that's the semi-annual coupon)
50,000 VND (= 5% × 1,000,000 VND face value, each year)
500,000 VND (= 50% × 1,000,000 VND, off by a decimal point)
5,000 VND (= 5% × 100,000 VND, wrong face value used)
quiz.explanation: Coupon = Coupon Rate × Face Value = 5% × 1,000,000 = 50,000 VND/year. If paid semi-annually, each 6-month period receives 25,000 VND. The coupon rate stays fixed for the whole term - it doesn't change even if market interest rates move.

quiz.question: Why is a bondholder considered safer than a stockholder when a company runs into financial trouble?
options: Bonds always pay a higher rate than the dividend shareholders receive
Shareholders only have voting rights, not a claim on the company's assets
A bondholder is a creditor, paid before shareholders if the company goes bankrupt
Bonds are listed, so they're easier to sell than stocks when cash is urgently needed
quiz.explanation: The order of payment priority in bankruptcy always places creditors (including bondholders) ahead of shareholders - this is the fundamental reason bonds are considered safer investments than stocks, even though the potential return is usually lower in exchange.

quiz.question: What three elements of a bond are fixed from the moment it's issued?
options: Yield, holding period, and the tax rate owed
Market price, yield, and trading volume
Credit rating, collateral, and the guarantor
Face value, coupon rate, and maturity date
quiz.explanation: These three figures are written into the contract and never change for the life of the bond. Everything else - price, yield, rating - moves around them, and that's why distinguishing coupon rate from YTM is the first step in reading any bond.

quiz.question: A bond with a 6% coupon is trading below face value. What does the real yield look like?
options: Higher than 6%, since you pay less money but still get the full coupon
Still exactly 6%, since the coupon rate is fixed
Lower than 6%, since the falling price reflects rising risk
Cannot be determined without knowing the remaining term
quiz.explanation: The coupon is calculated on face value so it doesn't change, but you pay less to receive it. A price below face value always pushes the yield above the coupon rate, and the reverse when buying above face value.

quiz.question: Why do bonds still carry risk despite being safer than stocks?
options: Because the coupon can be cut when the business runs into trouble
Because its price falls when market interest rates rise
Because bondholders lose the right to claim repayment after five years of holding
Because the repaid face value is adjusted downward for inflation
quiz.explanation: The coupon is a contractual obligation, so it isn't cut like a dividend can be. But holding a 4% bond when the market has risen to 7% means selling it at a loss - interest rate risk exists even when credit risk is zero.

keyTakeaways: Bond = lending money, receiving a coupon + principal at maturity
Bondholders rank ahead of stockholders in bankruptcy

practicePrompt.question: You buy a corporate bond with a face value of 100 million, a 5-year term, and an 8%/year coupon. What is the nature of this transaction, and what will you receive over the 5 years?
options: You're buying a share of ownership in the business, like buying stock, and will receive annual dividends
A bond is a loan: you receive an 8 million/year coupon and get your principal back at maturity
You're making a savings deposit with the business and can withdraw the money anytime without losing interest
You're buying an insurance contract, and the 8%/year is a premium you pay to the business
practicePrompt.explanation: Bond = lending money, receiving a coupon + principal at maturity. A bond buyer is a creditor (not an owner like with stocks), receiving periodic fixed interest (the coupon) and getting back the principal when the bond matures.

summary.keyIdea: Bond = lending money, receiving a coupon + principal at maturity
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a definition to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Look up a corporate bond or government bond currently being offered, and identify: what is the coupon rate, what is the face value, and what do you get back at maturity.
application.secondary: Reading a real offering document carefully makes the concept of a bond much less abstract.

sections.text: A bond is a standardised debt contract: the issuer - which could be a government or a business - borrows a fixed amount of money from investors, committing to pay periodic interest (the coupon) and repay the full principal (face value) on a set date (maturity). Unlike a stock - where you buy a share of company ownership - buying a bond is lending money, and the buyer becomes a creditor, not an owner.
The three core numbers of a bond

Every bond is defined by three elements: face value (the amount received back at maturity, typically 1 million or 100 million VND per lot), coupon rate (the fixed nominal interest rate calculated on face value), and maturity (the time until it comes due). **Example:** a bond with a face value of 1,000,000 VND, a coupon rate of 5%, and a 5-year term. Each year the investor receives 5% × 1,000,000 VND = 50,000 VND in interest, and after 5 years gets back exactly 1,000,000 VND in principal. If interest is paid semi-annually (common in the US), each 6-month period receives 25,000 VND.
Why bondholders rank ahead of shareholders

When a company goes bankrupt, remaining assets are distributed in a strict legal order: secured creditors first, then unsecured creditors (including most bondholders), then preferred shareholders, and finally common shareholders. A bondholder is a creditor - with a legal right to claim repayment first. A shareholder is a residual claimant - only receiving what's left after all debt obligations are settled, and in many bankruptcies, that residual amount is zero. This is exactly why bonds are considered a safer investment channel than stocks, even though the potential return in exchange is usually much lower.

items: Coupon = Coupon Rate × Face Value, fixed for the life of the bond regardless of market rate moves
Face value is the amount received back at maturity, not the bond's market purchase price
Government bonds (like Vietnam Treasury bonds) and corporate bonds both follow this same coupon - face value - maturity mechanism

lines: Understanding the three numbers - face value, coupon, maturity - is the first step to reading any bond.
Bankruptcy payment priority is the root reason bonds are safer than stocks.
